passages.text: ### Tina: the study cannot show what he says it shows

“No AI first” is useful (and also foundational to my UnBlooms framework). Learners should question, encounter evidence, activate prior knowledge, and generate an initial position before AI enters the process. Otherwise there is no independent reasoning to compare, critique, or refine. AI can provide material for critique, but the learner must still determine what counts as evidence, identify the assumptions, make the judgement, and explain the revision.

On the ‘learner as spectator’ point, this is what I mean: a student can ask AI for an answer, ask it to challenge that answer, and then ask which argument is stronger. The transcript contains all the features we associate with critical thinking: claims, counterclaims, evidence, and revision, but they were generated by the model. The learner may have witnessed an excellent argument without having constructed one.

We agree that repeated AI use may change learners, and that it deserves to be taken seriously rather than waved off. We agree it has not been shown. Until longitudinal evidence exists, carried out properly, learning design should preserve a visible human baseline before AI, human judgement during it, and human reflection after.
### **One thing to try in your classroom**

Give every student the same question. Have them fix their own position before any model sees it. That baseline does not have to be written: for some students writing is not the accessible route, and what matters is that the position exists and is recorded somehow, spoken, drawn or typed. Then have them ask the AI for the strongest possible case against them, and build the strongest case for the AI’s position themselves.
